When I began to have some dental issues, I was frustrated because I brushed and flossed my teeth daily. However, I knew I needed to do something quickly to help my gums and teeth to be stronger.

WHAT IS THE WATERPIK COMPLETE CARE SYSTEM LIKE?
(In doing my research, I found that I had a hard time figuring out how this system would work. It is for people in similar mindsets that I am writing this review)

WHAT TO DO FIRST
The first thing that you do is set up the area that you plan to put the unit. The footprint is similar to a women's size 5 shoe. It needs to be near an outlet which should be near the sink that you plan to use this system in. The unit has to be set up so that the water bin is closer to you. The tops of the unti all go in the opposite side of the unit where there are holes for them to stand up in.

The toothbrush base has to be charged up. Mine took overnight to reach full status with three lights on it. The lights will stay lit to let you know what the charge is after you use it for a few seconds.

HOW TO USE THIS UNIT
My family has a toothbrush head for each of us. I prefer the smaller head which comes in the unit. My daughter and husband each have a larger head that they use. They all have different colored rings on them so they can be told apart. You can also each have different reguiar tips for each of you if you prefer- this kit comes with two.

TOOTHBRUSH
When you first use the flosser, I find that it is best to brush our teeth first. You can set the toothbrush on gentle speed (sensitive teeth might like this one) or high speed. At first the high speed feels very intense, but in the long run, if you work up to it, it really does clean the teeth well.

Make sure that the toothbrush is in your mouth before turning it on. That will spare you splatters everywhere. Every 30 seconds the brush will pause briefly to let you know it is time to move to the next quadrant. I don't listen- I am a random brusher and go all over for 2 minutes. Once the brush is done, we remove the top and stand it up in the unit or other storage space.

THE FLOSSER
Using the flosser is not hard to do, it just takes some practice to learn your own method. First of all, the first time, the blue basin comes out of the unit. You rinse it and fill it with warm water. Then carefully replace the basin in the unit lining up the plug with the black seal on the unit. Once it is firmly placed in there, you put in the tip that you want and with the tip IN YOUR MOUTH BEFORE STARTING, you start the unit.

I recommend you start on gentle- the lowest of 10 settings- so that you can take some time to develop the method of use that works best for you. Once you have figured it out, then higher speeds are not as difficult to work with. We each have our own method of use. I tend to lean my head over the sink tilted slightly to the side. My husband turns his head completely to the side, letting the stream of water run out of the corner of his mouth. My daughter prefers to use it in private so I don't know what method she has worked out yet. She has used this with braces and now retainer and loves it.

There is a button on the flosser which pauses the stream so you can take it out of your mouth, rearrange it or turn it off without water spewing everywhere.

HOW WELL DOES THIS UNIT PERFORM?
My family rarely agrees completely on anything. We all have our own preferences and usually there are things we disagree on even if we agree. This system, however, has made us all rave as we all have seen a big change in our tooth and gum health. I am due for a cleaning after a long period of not being able to afford any, and since getting this system, I have found that my teeth have been looking cleaner and cleaner as I continue to use this.

Gum bleeding has been reduced to almost nothing for all of us. Our daughter's mouth hardware has been fabulously cleaned and she really loves the different heads. She uses the orthodontic tip for her teeth. My husband and I use the classic jet tip for now, and eventually I will use the pik pocket top once my teeth have been deep cleaned and settle down. I have also used the plaque seeker tip and found it to be very useful around the gum area.

To test this, I have used the waterpik flosser on medium after brushing my teeth on high speed. Then I floss with floss to test and see if anything was left. I have found one or two tiny pieces wedged in high up on the tooth, but that is it. My teeth usually hold a lot of debris, so this is quite impressive!

ANY DISLIKES?
The only things that I can say that we have not been crazy about has been trying to find the right manner to get the stream running out of the mouth with the least amount of mess. It is possible, but the way that the teeth are cleaned is so good, I am willing to put up with it. You will get wet using this- but it is not overwhelming. For people who really hate messiness in any form, this might not work out well for you.

THE BOTTOM LINE
This system comes with 2 classic tips, 1 plaque seeker tip, and pik pocket tip, a large toothbrush head and a compact toothbrush head. Between the things that this comes with, my family (with the addition of another brush head) has found this to be really revolutionary for our tooth and gum care. After use of both the brush and flosser, I have flossed with tooth floss and found almost nothing left every time.

We have not had any problems with the toothbrush not holding a charge, but we have had this under a month. I will update if we have any problems.

Although messy at times, our teeth have never been cleaner. I am very happy with this system so far. I will update with any new insight or information.

Here’s what I did:
1. Base coat, cure 30 seconds
2. Pink polish, cure 30 second
3. Repeat 2, if needed
4. Foil glue, cure 60 seconds (instructions say up to 120 seconds)
5. Apply foil (I used both a stick, and my fingers/nails to push it down, and tweezers to place the design)

7. Top coat, cure 60 seconds (only 30 needed, but did an extra 30 as a precaution just because there were so many layers)

The glue isn’t as thick as the base coat and top coat, so I used it sparingly to avoid getting it on my cuticles and fingers. I was concerned about the design where my nails curved and the foil wrinkled a lot when applying, but it didn’t noticeably affect the design. Comes with green, white, and black background as well as bags to hold them. Two large clamps to hold the corners and four small clips to hold the sides to the tripods. Everything seems pretty sturdy. For my small office, I only used two of the four crossbars.

So after testing it out for a while I have some suggestions for anyone else who wants to get a background setup:
Use WHITE for photography (still life and portraits). Use GREEN for video (especially streaming). Use BLACK for either one as long as you're not trying to mask out of the background or do chroma key. I think black would be ideal for a lot of my videos...give them a more professional look.

Another bit of advice - Pick up some of those table cloth weights you use on picnic tables to attach along the bottom to hold this completely flat. Either that or iron the cloth really well before use.

Also - Use background lighting. Light the screen BRIGHTLY as well as getting decent light on the subject. Eliminates shadows and hides wrinkles in the canvas. If you've got a big diffuse light box, possibly a good idea to just use the white or black backgrounds.

Overall I'm impressed. I've learned a lot about photography and videos by having background screens. It's not as complicated as I thought at all, but figuring out the basics first takes a bit of practice. Great kit for the price.

We have multiple TVs, so I picked this up to receive minimal channels on a TV that we didn't have an antenna for. It is not on par with the two amplified antennas we have and use, but it gets us a few local channels, and for the price, that's all I was looking for.

This unamplified antenna gets 28 channels, my [[ASIN:B00IF70T4M 1byone Amplified HDTV Antenna - 50 Mile Range with Detachable Amplifier Power Supply for the Highest Performance and 10ft Coax Cable]] gets 32, and the [[ASIN:B00DHKKI16 Mohu Leaf 50 Indoor HDTV Antenna (Certified Refurbished)]] gets 42. While those numbers suggest that the 1byone offered only a marginal improvement over the unamplified antenna, that is not true. Both amplified antennas make both ABC and CBS consistently watchable, while this unamplified was prone to "no signal" outages on those channels periodically.

If you're looking to have access to a minimal number of channels on a TV for local news, or know the channels you care about are close enough for an unamplified antenna, this certainly provides some bang for the buck based on the low cost. But if you're interested in getting a good number of channels, I recommend springing for the Mohu.

The editor of a major women's magazine recently touted the powder version of this product; mostly she liked being able to order online and have it delivered to her house. Because of sensitive skin, I have used liquid detergents for years, even making my own low-suds recipe for awhile but gave that up when I discovered a major eco-friendly brand that was low-sudsing and didn't irritate my skin. After reading about this product, I went to the Charlie's Soap website and tracked the 32-oz liquid container (for $10) to a local store. It was a bit pricey for the size, but since it is just my husband and me (three adult sons are in and out very irregularly), I decided to give it a try. The first thing I liked about the bottle was the built-in measurer with markings in both ounce and milliliter. Squeeze the bottle and the soap goes up the tube on the side of the bottle into the measurer and you pour it directly into your washer's soap dispenser, then the cap screws back on. No separate, messy lid or spillage to deal with. There is a second cap to unscrew, with a regular large opening, because this handy container is refillable from the gallon jug. The packaging says to run a couple loads with rags to clean the old detergent out of the washer; I didn't do that so my first load was bit sudsy, so I ran the load several times to get out any old suds. I couldn't believe how naturally soft my clothes were (I haven't used fabric softener in years since we have softened water). I also like that there is no added fragrance, and the soap doesn't have any particular natural fragrance. The ingredients listed are washing soda, coconut oil and other natural cleaners. Also, my HE washer is very clean now and doesn't have that stale, mildewed smell (I always leave the door open when not in use). Charlie's Soap is made for HE washers, and the directions say to use no more than one ounce per load, even a large load. I do that, and even with softened water the soap generates practically no suds. If there are suds, it's because I'm washing clothes or other items that have old detergent in them. I cannot say enough good things about Charlie's Soap, and considering that I paid $10 for the 32-oz container, this four-gallon multipack is quite a bargain. I also signed up for the six-month autosubscribe (the maximum time, which I will adjust if necessary) so there was another small discount for that. Yes, it does seem a bit weird to order laundry soap online, but considering the savings and that it is delivered to my door (in a box that my cats love), I got over the weirdness pretty quickly.

I've never really been a fan of wet-install screen protectors, but this one changed my mind.

Before beginning, I took two extra minutes to watch the installation video Skinomi provides on YouTube. The process looked to be about what I expected, but watching the video was helpful nonetheless. One little bit of confusion, though, is that the printed installation instructions in the package say to wait a minimum of 4 to 5 hours before handling the device, but the video says 10 to 12 hours. They both agree, however, that the "curing" or "setting" can be accelerated with a hair dryer on warm (not hot). More on the hair dryer later. There's also some disagreement in the directions about how long it will take for "microbubbles and imperfections" to clear up - one place says 2 to 3 days, a different place says 3 to 5 days.

So, I took all that to mean A) the longer you wait to handle the device, the better off you'll be and B) exercise some patience while waiting for the bubbles and imperfections to work themselves out. I also took the advice to install the protector before going to bed, so it can continue curing while you're asleep - which helps you avoid the temptation of playing with the device before the protector is cured.

The actual installation went exactly the way the video shows, so I'm not going to spend the time to do a play-by-play here - just have a look at the video (go to Skinomi's web site, look for "installation" near the bottom of the screen). The part of the protector over the "edge" screen didn't want to stick at first. Remembering the tip from the video that the edge part of the protector needs to be less wet, I used my still-wet fingers to squeegee some of the application solution out of that part and then it adhered to the "Edge" with no additional problem.

After "squeegeeing" the solution out from under the screen protector, I had one tiny air bubble and two spots of "imperfections" - looked like scuffs for lack of a better description. I should have taken photos. Oh, well. Not being quite sure about 4 to 5 hours or 10 to 12 hours, I pulled out my wife's hair dryer and went to work. The key here is to get the protector warm enough to accelerate the "setting" process, but not hot enough to damage it or your device. I kept it warm to the touch for about 5 minutes and then let it cool off. Then applied more heat for another 5 minutes and so-on for about 5 or 6 cycles. Through the process, I could see some improvements; the blemishes were fading slightly each time. It probably doesn't really need as much attention as I gave it, but I wanted to be sure that it would be well and fully set when I got up the next morning so I could use my phone without worrying about the protector coming undone.

My efforts with the hair dryer must have been worth it - I woke up the next morning to a PERFECT, flawless screen protector.

Visibly, the screen protector has a slight orange-peel look to it. It's not very prominent (unlike an "Invisible Shield" which is quite noticeable), but it's plainly visible in the right light. Nevertheless, the protector does NOT appear to interfere with the clarity of the screen at all.

When using my finger to operate the phone, the touch is nearly indistinguishable from bare glass (also very unlike an "Invisible Shield). There is, however, a somewhat different feel to using the S Pen for swiping, dragging, or writing - it's a little more "draggy," sort of like when you walk through knee-deep water. It's not different enough for me to want to take the protector off, but if you want to maintain the "original" feel of the S Pen on bare glass, then this protector might not be the best one for you.

After using the S Pen for a little while, I could see I left some fairly visible troughs and valleys in the protector from the pen strokes. Living up to the claim of being self-healing, most of these disappeared overnight. I have little doubt that this protector will be able to take a good bit of abuse over its life and it carries a lifetime warranty in case it doesn't.

After all is said and done, I'm happy with this purchase and would not hesitate recommending this protector to anyone. I docked one-star, though, because the printed directions and the installation video seem to be "on different pages" about how long the device should be left to sit.

My wife got this for me for my 40th birthday. Clearly, a subtle signal that I needed to workout more and was already over the hill and needed a heart monitor. She also got it because I'm a bit "techy" and the other reviews stated that you could track an immense amount of information with the GPS and monitor.

I absolutely love my Garmin. I use it all the time when I run and bike and religiously upload the information. It is outstanding for heart zone workouts and maintaining pace and can really give you a sense of how you're tracking on your regular routes. The upload and sync is easy. Over the 18 months I've had this, I have transitioned from PC to Mac and both syncs work well. PC actually works better and the application has better rendering. This is actually the only knock I have. I would have expected the Mac version to be more polished. That said, all the data is there and can be easily reviewed.

The GPS tracks well. The initial satellite sync can take a while, but I've found that if I bypass it by hitting the mode button, it will still pick up satellites and track pace and location relatively quickly. The display can be easily customized to show the information that you care about and there's a lot of workouts that you can program to augment your training.

The heart monitor works well. I've run into two issues when cycling where if I have a layer, like a wick shirt for running or biking, on, it can cause a strange heartbeat spike. This is actually due to some initial static that gets generated with some of the workout shirts, but can be resolved by sweating, or (what I do) licking your hand and wiping a bit of spit on the underside of the sensor before working out. I'm like accurate stats and seeing a 197 heart rate is disconcerting to me. I have not had to replace any battery on the monitor yet and it's comfortable and sturdy.

I absolutely love this thing and to this day, my wife and I agree, that it is one of the best gifts ever.

I read a lot of reviews.
1. The little tab for opening them is only on one corner and hard to see. So, get a Sharpie or a paint pen, and mark that tab. I did this, and put them on the shelf so that tab is always going to be where I need it. For other people, seeing it will help.
2. The label on the top seemed to be a deal breaker and a point of great vexation for many. I don't care because the shelf is only 5.5" or so high and I will never see the lid. But in the interest of science, kitchen science, to be exact, I decided to try to solve that problem, since one buyer said that GooGone interacted badly with the plastic.
I applied a layer of mayonnaise and let it sit overnight. Then put a paper towel over my thumb and used my nail to come at the label from all sides, causing the edges to lift. I next pulled those edges back over the label, not straight up, removing big sections, and repeated the process using peanut butter. Really, either one works. Oils break down the adhesives, but aren't strong enough, obviously, to interfere with the plastic.
Although this took time, in less than 48 hours, I had a clear box lid. There is a small dot in the center from where the plastic was poured into the mould.

As a programmer, I'll second (and third, and fourth) that making the switch to 4K is something you'll do and you'll never go back.

The visuals/brightness/colors are just fine on this monitor for programming. No bad pixels, and supports the full 60 Hz 4:4:4 (with sufficient graphics card) which would be my only concern along those lines.

One thing worthy of note: At first I assumed I'd be using this monitor for programming by placing many application windows on the screen at the same time - kind of like 'FOUR 1920x1080 monitors in one'. I even tested different window manager programs, and went with WinDivvy (it's great - simple, and works so that with a single key combination you can pop any window to any size / position).

However, quickly I shifted into my current mode of work: With the 4K, I now use the monitor in PORTRAIT mode, and only have ONE application window showing at a time, filling the entire screen. Yes, that means that I still have as many Alt + Tabs as I did with my 1920 x 1080, but you can fit an INCREDIBLE amount of vertical text on the screen with a 38040 x 2160 in PORTRAIT mode. Just a few Page Up/Page Downs can navigate through an entire thousands-of-lines source code file.

Seeing so much code on the screen at one time makes the mental effort SO much easier. I recommend this monitor in PORTRAIT mode for programmers.

Packaging

Directions
-These were really fantastic. They lay things out in detail but also keep it brief for the many different options available. Turn on the bluetooth mode on your phone. I found the app "Da Fit App" from the product description, though the directions only show a QR code. From there it was opening the app and doing a quick profile setup (Sex, Height, Weight, Birth Year). It automatically scanned for the phone and the letters displayed on the screen and it was the only one shown so that was quick. I do wish it would pop up a notification that the pairing was successful but there is a watch icon in the app at the bottom. The App
-Very well laid out and some details were provided earlier but you can adjust the notifications you receive and it all pairs through Bluetooth so as long as they are on (and you accept push notifications on the phone) you'll receive the notifications on the phone. You can make a lot of the adjustments you want through the watch, but the app can allow for a faster level to set all at once.

The Modes
Phone calls, sleep (need to leave on during sleep), heart rate test, steps, training (stopwatch), blood pressure, SpO2 Test, Weather, Reminders, Shutter (photos/video), start/stop songs, Alarms, Timer, Stopwatch, Theater Mode (turns off vibrating and brightness), Move reminders, Drink reminders (stay healthy), Health reminders (menstrual, pregnancy, gender health).

The watch will sync to your timezone once the app is set and you can also get weather notifications which I set inside the app.

I have owned this dryer for two and a half years and it still work perfectly.

All dryers seem to be the same with a fan, a heating element a stay cool body and some controls. This one has a powerful heating element (1875 watts), and a good fan (for its size). The purpose of a hair dryer is not to heat up the hair to boil away the water, but to speed up the evaporation process of drying by exposing the hair to a stream of hot air. The faster the stream and the warmer the air, the more evaporation occurs. Where this dryer differs is in the body that has a longer and narrower nozzle that is about one inch wide. This forces a much stronger blast of air (at least on high speed) that is not a wide as those dryers with a wide nozzle.

If your hair is fine, colored, permed or naturally curly, you would want a different dryer with a wider nozzle to diffuse the heat so that the hair dries more slowly at a cooler temperature. That may make the hair less likely to frizz and it may give the hair more volume.

This dryer makes the nozzle narrow and thus helps to concentrate the heat into one spot in order to make the hair it blows on dry rapidly. You can adjust the fan speed and the temperature, but not the concentration of the air flow.

So, if you have regular hair or (like me) are a guy that just wants to dry their hair rapidly, this is the dryer for you. Put it on high speed and high heat and it is extremely fast.

My favorite method is to file dry feet, and then cover your feet with a combination of coconut oil and emu oil. Leave big cotton socks on overnight, and wake up to gorgeous feet.

On the good side, they do exactly what they say they will do. If you follow instructions and are patient for the next week or so, at least in my case, I started shedding like crazy, just like most other users. My only problem with this product is that if you have those really thick heel calluses, the acid just won't go deep enough to lift the skin.
The photo shows about 15 days after a peel. My foot is really soft but as you can see, there is still that thick hard callus and some residual peeling on the side.
In my case, the peeling doesn't start for at least 7 days.

So, if you are like me, don't retire your cheese grater type file or your diamond file just yet. But for the rest of your feet, this baby foot peel is unbelievable. You really will have softer feet than you ever thought possible.

Phosphatidylserine is created in your body, but supplementing with it can help with brain function. It might help with ADHD symptoms as well, and PS pairs well with fish oil. I don’t notice much benefit from PS, so I take it based on the research studies more than personal experience.

Not much, if any, research has been done on the effect of PS derived from sunflowers, which is what is in this product. The studies showing the benefit from PS supplementation were done using PS derived from different sources, notably cows, then, later on, soybeans. If you want a product backed by scientific studies, you should get a soybean-based one, such as the products NOW, Solgar, Nootropics Depot, Doctor’s Best, Thorne, and many others sell. This is not a standardized product and the life form it is extracted from impacts the chemical makeup of the supplement. I would expect soy-based PS to work similar to sunflower PS, but these are different from PS derived from animals.

I tested all 6 cables for proper USB-C compliance using my Google Nexus 6P phone with the CheckR app. The app said all 6 cables failed compliance (see uploaded photo), which means they don't have the necessary 56 kohm pullup resistor. This has been a big issue with USB A-to-C cables for the last couple of years, so I'm surprised that Sabrent didn't test this before releasing these cables. The key thing is that these A-to-C cables are supposed to have a 56k ohm resistor for safety, so that the client device tries to draw only as much electricity as the host can provide. Without this resistor in place, the phone can try to draw too much power, potentially frying your laptop, charger and phone.

It's unfortunate that these cables are not compliant, because otherwise they are good quality. They have nylon fabric covering, a seamless connector on the USB-C side from deep-draw extrusion (instead of just stamped), and a velcro cable keeper attached to each one. The connections are secure without much wiggle, and the length is perfect for connecting to an external battery pack. I really like the quality of these cables, but I will not be using them due to the risk of them destroying my devices.

I also tested this out with terminating connection from the laptops to bluetooth headphones, a chromecast device, and just a single tracert to a google dns server. In all of the tests the connections were dropped. I also used an iPad 8th gen and my Samsung S8 with outbound calls to check alongside the laptop if I could store them in the bag during travel. I'm not paranoid (famous last words). No, really, I welcome my personal assistant overlords. My family is pretty vanilla. So it only creeps me out a little when my husband and I have "test" discussions about things we don't talk about, don't search the internet for, and would never actually buy in a million years only to see such items pushed to us in advertising feeds. Is one of our assistants listening when it is supposed to be asleep? If so, which one? All three of the majors are in our house. Both of the cats have turned Siri on by walking across my laptop. And Alexa hears her name sometimes inexplicably. Maybe it's my husband's Long Island accent?

Or maybe it is just randomness and the assistants are functioning as advertised. Either way, I won't be getting rid of them anytime soon. The Echo Plus recognized all but two of my smart bulbs and found all of my switches and everything else that still works (old WeMo stuff went offline over a year ago when Belkin pushed a firmware upgrade and killed their wifi connections). It has controlled them flawlessly so far, and this has allowed me to free up the ethernet ports I'd dedicated to several different hubs.

My Echo devices are the ones we use most around here, both because the house runs on Amazon Prime and Subscribe and Save (I have lupus and cannot easily shop in the real world) AND because the Echos allow me to reach my teenager and tell him things whether he wants to hear them or not. He can ignore my texts and refuse to answer the phone, but Alexa lets me yell at him from anywhere in the world. (And the app lets me see his history of ridiculous teenaged boy questions - unlike Siri, Alexa is not a potty mouth and does not like it when you are.)

On the downside, Alexa won't give you suggestions if she doesn't know something. She just gives you an Elizabeth Jennings (The Americans) type, "Hmmm," and a disappointed note.

The Echo Plus also seems to "hear" better and have fewer false activations. And the sound is better for music - by a surprising amount. So, if Alexa has a place in your home, the Echo Plus is a good way to get her. Four stars. I'd give five if the wake word were more customizable.

This is an excellent indoor antenna. I purchased it in order to get the major broadcast networks because I am in the process of stopping our satellite service and streaming everything instead. Yesterday, the antenna arrived. I immediately set it up and put it behind the television (an LG smart TV) so that it wasn't visible (my wife would complain). I then ran the 'auto scan' function to detect over the air stations. We live in central Houston and I assumed that I would easily get the major network stations. The first auto scan produced 48 stations. However, of the major networks, only PBS (3 stations) and Fox were detected by the auto scan.

I then ran the auto scan again and this time 76 stations were identified. Of the majors, PBS, Fox and CBS were found but not NBC and ABC. So, I moved the antenna a few inches away and re-ran the auto scan. This time, 86 stations were identified including all the majors. I moved the antenna back to the original position and I have had no problem in seeing any of those broadcast stations.

In other words, in order to get all the broadcast stations that you want, you may have to run the auto scan multiple times. I can't complain about getting 86 stations, most of which I have never heard of (and certainly are not included with our satellite subscription). I probably won't watch the vast majority but it's nice to know they are there.

So I've been buying whey protein for more than ten years now, and figured I'd try something new with the casein. I don't need it, as some do for health reasons, I just wanted to give it a try. I purchased the Chocolate.

Consistency-wise - it thickens much more quickly, and to a much greater degree than whey protein - maybe even twice as much. A single scoop needs about 16oz of water. If you get the ratio right, it has a bit of a chalky consistency, but its not unpalatable, at least for me.

Flavor-wise - atypical, but not too much so. It has the same flavor notes as whey protein, just in different proportions. Lacks protein bitterness, which is nice, but does have a bit of that "protein mustiness" you sometimes taste in the older style protein shakes.

Gastro-wise - atypical, at least for me. It doesn't move like regular whey protein and disrupts my usual schedule. No bloating, no discomfort, but interferes a little bit with regularity. Unusual odor - like a burnt eraser.

Value - decent value, middle of the road in protein content. There's no reason to pick this over whey proteins if you have the option.

I guess I'd recommend it for people who want to mix it up a bit with their shake/stack, and if you can only take this kind of protein, know that it is pretty similar to the regular whey-type. Otherwise, stick with the standard whey isolate family of protein powders.

[[VIDEOID:b21ba802df7fea83af659db90aa0851b]] Aside from one problem, these are perhaps the most useful, well-designed and economical C-stands I've ever seen.

Starting at the bottom, it's a turtle style, meaning the center column is removable. This allows for easy transport.

But here's the problem: the column's diameter where it slides into the turtle is NOT STANDARD DIAMETER. It's 1.095". It should be 1.125" (1-1/8"). This means standard accessories will not fit into the turtle base.

Nothing's more clumsy than a folded C-stand. The best way to transport a standard single-piece C-stand is with a custom cart made for the job like the [[ASIN:B01DMUNL28 C-Stand Cart (cart only, stands not included)]] for only $461. And you'll need a lift-gate truck to move the filled cart about.

With two-piece C-stands like this Neewer beauty, you take the center column off, fold up the turtle base and carry them separately on any cart. The turtle base folds using spring pressure detents. The legs, when in the detents, are splayed properly. They don't have a sliding "crazy leg" for uneven terrain like the [[ASIN:B003E4793K Avenger A2033LKIT Steel 40-Inch Sliding Leg C-Stand with Grip Kit (Chrome)]]. Use these on flat floors.

Because the turtle base does not accept a 1-1/8" column, it cannot be used as a low-boy stand. A gazinta like the Kupo junior-to-baby adapter [[ASIN:B006JHK80K Kupo Adapter, Junior to Baby, 1-1/8-Inch Stud to 5/8-Inch Stud, KG006312]], will not drop it into the turtle base. This is very disappointing. I actually bought a Kupo 20" column so I could have two different heights, but the Kupo will not fit into this Neewer.

Moving up is the unique center post. It has two strong internal springs that act like shock absorbers. If you have a heavy light up in the air or a backdrop suspended between two of these stands and some amateur loosens one of the lock handles too much without holding up the weight, the column will certainly slide all the way down. If he's lucky, he doesn't have his hand on the center post because a normal stand will pinch and/or crush it. This stand will stop short and bounce on the spring. The best I've seen on other stands is a thick rubber O-ring that softens the descent only a little. These springs may even save an expensive bulb's filament from damage as the lighting unit bounces off the spring, but does not bottom out. Other stands may have these features, but this Neewer is the first I've seen. Check out the video.

There is a neoprene sleeve for gripping the post. It's a good, thick, solid grip that should last.

The two extension sections elevate and lower smoothly, controlled by large friction knobs. The castings are solid and well finished with no sharp edges, secured to the center post by a large set screw. An Allen wrench is included should this set screw loosen over time or you want to take the column apart.

Moving up to the gobo arm, it's strong steel with a 5/8" spud at both ends. One spud end has a 1/4-20 thread on it and the other end has a 3/8-16 thread on it. With these two threads, plus the 5/8" spuds, you can mount just about anything. Both thread ends are protected by small rubber caps, which you'll probably lose after the first shoot unless you put them in your pocket.

The arm has two gobo clamps: one to adapt the arm to the stand and one for holding accessories like scrims, reflectors, softboxes or flags. Both slide the full length of the arm. You can add a set screw (not included) if you desire to lock them to the arm. The clamps have fine-tooth interlocking faces instead of a leather or composite friction washer. If you loosen the clamp knob sufficiently, the teeth will clear each other without wearing themselves off. Once locked together, I cannot imagine the gobo arm sagging and changing its angle, no matter how much the light weighs. Both clamps are nicely finished and have large, easily gripped locking knobs. The tightening washers are well-greased to prevent galling and are shaped like miniature tripod ball mounts -- a cup-shaped bottom fits into a matching cup-shaped hollow in the clamp. This allows the two halves of the clamp to move to accommodate different diameters of flag pins, but still tighten securely. Easier seen than explained.

Packaging was excellent: bubble wrap around every piece, then into Styrofoam shipping blocks, then into an inner cardboard box then two of those boxes into an outer cardboard box. I pity the UPS guy who had to deliver the thing, but both stands arrived in perfect condition. I set them up in a few minutes.

For about $105 each, the only way I'd be more pleased is if the turtle had a standard socket size. Had to take a star off. And now I have to send back my Kupo 20" column %^$#$$!!

This antenna is about 16" long, but it does seem to do what it is supposed to. It looks a bit weird attached to the camera because it is long, But as far as I can tell it works pretty good. I put this antenna on and bingo it connected right away. I don't think it can punch through steel and the fiberglass door helps I'm sure, but still, the standard antenna wouldn't get there and this one does. I can't speak to how far it will extend the range and there are a lot of factors that can impact that, but I am convinced that it will get you farther than the standard antenna.

I plan on trying some experimenting this coming Summer with an outdoor camera to see just how far it will extend the range line of sight.

I will just add that among the various factors that can impact wireless range, other wireless traffic in the area can be the biggest one to cause problems. Sometimes different channels work better than others. This antenna will not solve all problems by any means, but it should help. Whether or not it is enough can not be predicted reliably. Your specific set of conditions means a lot. Sometimes you can also get high gain antennas for your router too. These might even fit depending on the connector. Keep in mind that increasing the range of your router also makes your router more vulnerable to being intercepted. Use security.

If it weren't so fiddly to use, I would really love this RSVP SHUCK DELUXE CORN STRIPPER. The product's clear plastic outer tube is both its best and its worst feature. The best, because the tube catches all of the stripped corn kernels, and is easy to empty. The worst, because the tube must be opened and closed for every single ear of corn; each ear of corn must be carefully positioned inside the tube; and the yellow cap at the bottom of the tube has screw threads that run in the "wrong" direction. (To unscrew something, the mantra is "righty tightey, lefty loosey"--but this tube opens when turned right, and closes when turned left. Probably it's designed this way so it won't unscrew when the corer is twisted.)

The stainless steel "corer" is sharp, and it cuts the kernels off the cob with very little downward pushing effort. However, it misses all the kernels at the narrow end of the ear. The gadget is a little confusing at first, but simple to use once you understand how it works. You cut the kernels off by twisting the scalloped yellow part that's attached to the stainless steel corer; then you use the knobbed yellow part to push the stripped cob out of the corer. It's easiest if you take the knobbed part out before you strip the corn kernels off the cob. All of the corn stripper parts are sturdy, and they are all dishwasher safe.

This RSVP Corn Stripper is slightly more efficient than my [[ASIN:B000V78JGO OXO Good Grips Corn Stripper]], which has to be emptied several times for each ear of corn, and is a bit awkward to take apart and reassemble each time. However, my favorite tool for this job is the [[ASIN:B006GDRD9G Zyliss Corn Stripper]], which strips an entire ear of corn completely with 4 or 5 quick downward strokes (when you hold an ear of corn over a bowl or plate, you don't need either a tube (RSVP) or a container (OXO) to catch the stripped kernels).

Because it's fiddly and not the best available tool for the job, I rate this well-made product at 3 stars ("It's okay" on the official Amazon scale).

I needed a phone case for my new phone, the Samsung Galaxy S22 Ultra. I searched and searched and searched. Many websites (Amazon included) and other dubiously trustworthy sites. I wanted a flip cover, so I did not have to buy a screen protector. I wanted it real leather, because anything you want to last needs to be real leather. It needed to look smart, potentially hold a credit card or two, some bills perhaps, and be easy to use. This KEZiHOME phone case spoke to me, caught my eye, and no matter what other cases I looked at, I kept going back to this one. So I bought it, and am very happy I did.

First, I am a stickler for protecting leather, something people that have read my other reviews should know. I tried the phone case for fit on my new phone, then immediately took the phone out. I used Pecard Leather Dressing (purchased here on Amazon) a product that I have used for all my leather goods for over 2 decades. I put 2 coats on the leather phone case - the first coat was totally absorbed after 24 hours, the second coat was mostly absorbed after an additional 24 hours, at which point I used a soft cloth to buff the surface to a beautiful shine. The case was now protected, waterproof, and will withstand the ravages of handling it daily.

After that second coat dried, I put the lens protectors that I had purchased (previously reviewed here on Amazon) onto the phone, and slipped it into this gorgeous leather case. It gleamed in my hand, and was soft and sturdy at the same time. The leather dressing enhanced the deepness of the leather color, and turned the rather nice phone case into a work of art.

I have been using the phone in its new case for the last couple of days, and must say that is is fantastic. the case is easy to open, easy to close, and everything on the phone is fully functional. The S-pen is easy to remove from the phone, the camera works beautifully, and the sound (both receiving and transmitting) is outstanding. The two-toned color is part of the phone case's charm - it lends a sense of specialness to the case, and makes a plain case interesting. As a note - the manufacture left a cut-out piece of the case from where the camera cut-out occurred - probably not on purpose, but it let me examine the leather, and I can honestly report that real leather is used on this case.

All in all, a great case, at a wonderful price on Amazon, and I could not be happier. Thank you KEZiHOME, I hope to be able to use you on future purchases.

I had a prior version of this keyboard (the Microsoft Natural Ergonomic Keyboard 3000) for my office PC. It did admirably, but after a year or so, my wrists were starting to hurt IN SPITE OF the ergonomics helping. This one is better rated. So far, it has helped, but it took at least a week of use just for my hands to BEGIN to get used to the differences. I'd do a pro/con list, but I'm not sure there are any "cons" as compared to "issues to expect" if you buy this keyboard.

1. Expect a steep learning curve to get used to the layout. The "bend" in this keyboard is significant, and it will take time for your fingers to get used to hitting the right keys on a consistent basis. Give it one or two weeks of regular use before deciding if you like it or not. You can't know in a couple of days if it's helping you because you do need to re-learn your hand placement and fingering to some degree.

2. There is a physical break in the left and right hand keys. This "no man's land" means you need to unlearn using the wrong hand for the wrong keys because you will either miskey or just hit nothing when you go to use your right hand to it the G key (or a similar situation). Likewise, some of the keys have an odd shape that takes getting used to. I had considerable issue getting used to hitting V and B correctly. Again, this is all about relearning how to keyboard properly. My best tip is to avoid looking at the keyboard while typing. For me, looking at the keyboard made it harder compared to just backspacing and repeating until I got it right. Passwords are about the only thing where I still watch what keys I strike.

3. This keyboard is wider and "taller" than most. If you use a keyboard tray, clearing it might pose and issue (see next point below). You will likely have less room for your mouse as well, but I found it something I could live with.

4. The keyboard has three (maybe four) resting positions. There's a removable front skirt that elevates the front. There are the standard rear folding supports to elevate the rear. So, that's resting flat (none), rear elevated, front elevated, and both elevated. Lying flat, the keyboard works fine with my keyboard tray. Set the way I find it's most comfortable for me, I can only push the tray in halfway before the keyboard hits the desk. This isn't a deal breaker for me, so I'll live with it. You keyboard tray may need to allow at least 3 inches of vertical clearance to not have an issue with this keyboard.

This ZINUS MODERN STUDIO COLLECTION RECTANGULAR COFFEE TABLE AND TWO SQUARE SIDE TABLES, currently selling for about $100 on Amazon, provides excellent value for someone furnishing an apartment for the first time (or furnishing any short-term residence). The tables look pretty good--you get used to the reddish-brown wood finish--and they hold a lot of stuff because they have tops with shelves below.

To be sure, these tables are NOT sturdy, heavy-duty tables that adults (or children) can stand on, or that can be loaded up with seriously heavy items. The metal frames are strong; but the tops and lower shelves consist of a metal frame that encloses a thin sheet of wood supported by a thick wire underneath. Also, the tops and shelves are bolted to the frames with only a single bolt at each corner (8 bolts per table).

Nevertheless, the tables will hold lightweight tubs or boxes (at least 15-20 lbs., probably more) that distribute their weight evenly across the top or shelf. If used as intended, as a coffee table and side tables, the grouping will easily hold lamps, books, magazines, remotes, coffee and food trays, and other stuff that you need to get up off the floor.

Assembly is about as easy as it gets. All the necessary hardware and tools (bolts and a hex wrench) are included, and the instruction sheet drawings are crystal clear. Each of these three pieces took me 10 minutes to assemble, for 30 minutes total.

One cautionary note: Do inspect your tabletops and shelves carefully. One of my side table pieces had a barely noticeable crack that was clearly caused by some direct blow suffered during shipping. I decided to use that piece as a lower shelf, rather than to request a replacement, but only because the crack was nearly invisible and didn't seem to seriously weaken the shelf.

I am pretty impressed with this case. Please keep in mind that it isn't a 30 dollar armored tank-proof case, etc.

It has two layers. First is a shock-absorbing silicone on the inside. Then a tough case that diffuses shock and resists puncture on the outside.

They seemed to have done a good job engineering this one.

The outside of the case is slightly rubberized. This gives a better grip than normal...maybe a tad better than the original cheapo case. If you think about it though, imagine if it was really sticky/tacky. Youd have a hard time slipping it into your pocket. So I think this is a good compromise.

The power slot is actually big enough for chargers, instead of not fitting like the cheapo case. Ditto with the other slots. I am happy with this improvement.

Power button and volume buttons work really well. The case is cutout there, with the silicon overlayed, which makes it much easier to find the buttons by feel. Ive had no issues with it compressing any buttons or being hard to push...they are easier to push but with no false positives so far.

The silicon case comes over the top of the phone and wraps around, just about up to where the actual screen starts. It has a tight fit which should help keep the corners of your screen protector in place, and reduce dust and splooge that gets underneath the protectors.

The only improvement I would want is a bit better grip. A cutout below the buttons where you hold it would be beneficial. A few dabs of rubber cement or something might help improve grip in the places where you typically hold it. I might give that a try...dunno how well stuff will stick to the case.

I expect that no one is going to use a stylus 100% of the time with their touch screen. There are, however, some times when a stylus is more convenient than using your finger. Drawing objects freehand is a common example. Another example is when you need to precisely move objects around the screen (eg in a CAD program) and this is difficult with your finger because your finger blocks your view of the target area.

There are many many touch screen stylus for sale on Amazon. Some cost less than 50 cents each. All the latest stylus have similar round soft touch rubber tips. All seem to work about the same. This iHome stylus doesn't seem to work any better than the others that I have tried.

The iHome stylus is better looking than most of the competition because of the long slim shape with silver-tone accents. Some of the cheap ones look very plasticy (though they do work just as well). Some other stylus are fatter, which makes them easier to grip if you have large hands.

The built-in ball-point pen is a feature that most other stylus do not have. The pen works well, though I do not know how easy ink refills will be to find. There is no literature in the package about what refills it can use.

Is this product worth $15? I have to say no, but I'm a cheapskate. You can decide on value for yourself, but look at the competition first.

I support a lot of systems around the world that use Windows-based PCs and I run into a lot of viruses and trojans on those systems. For that reason it is really important to me to have a write-protectable drive that is not subject to being compromised by BadUSB, but something on which I can periodically update files as some of my software is updated. The Kanguru drives excel in both these areas. This isn't my first experience with Kanguru drives; I have some of the older, smaller-capacity models that are only USB 2.0 speed and not quite as secure.

Because I have the older drives I am accustomed to the older User Interface for logging in to the drive. It was simple, would allow you to use whatever you want as a password (I prefer to use very long passphrases, about 80 characters), and very simply opened the drive for use afterwards. The new UI throws most of that away. Now, you are forced to use what Kanguru believes to be the more secure model of UPPER and lower case, plus at least one number and one special character. Contrary to popular belief this scenario is actually less secure because people have a hard time remembering passwords in that format so will either write them down and/or reuse the same password for many things (banking, work, etc.). Further that, once you can figure out your password and log in you have to wait while the UI tries to connect to an anti-virus server, and deal with a couple dialogs if/when it can't. You cannot turn off this feature. It's nice that it's included but one should be able to turn it off, particularly when dealing with systems that have no Internet connection as a security precaution. It's so bad that my immediate impulse was to return the drive. Instead I kept it but I don't use it nearly as much as the older one which was much smaller and frequently filled up. When this one fails or becomes too small for my needs I won't be going back to Kanguru for a replacement. I'd rather go back to carrying a wallet of DVDs.

So, a Five-plus star product hampered by a two-star User-Unfriendly Interface equals 4 stars.

I'm at an age where things can happen that result in the need (sometimes temporary) for mobility devices like a rollator. I'm facing knee replacement surgery in the next year or so, for example. (Years of dancing professionally and hardcore equestrian sports can take a toll on joints). My orthopedic doc had already mentioned that I'd need to have one of these on hand, so having the opportunity to check one out up close and personal came at a good time.

First things first: I really like this. It's much higher quality than I expected.

It's a nice looking contraption -- deep burgundy with black trim, very solid and sturdy. I found assembly to be relatively simple, and I'm an older DIY-challenged female. I'm also what could be described as "Junoesque" -- a bit more acreage and tonnage than I should be carrying, but below the max weight limit of this device (yeah, I'm working on it -- I've lost 75 lbs in the past 18 months). Once assembled, I was able to use it both for mobility and for seating with no worries about stability. It's solid, for sure. The seat is 21" from the floor, which is perfect for me -- my doc said it had to be at least 18", so we're good. I'm also tall-ish (5'8") -- someone who is very short might have difficulty with the seat height.

My house is all on one level with no stairs inside or outside the house except a small (4") step down from the dining room to the outdoor patio. Getting from garage to kitchen has a couple of "bumps" where the flooring changes from linoleum to carpet to quarry tile, and the 6" wheels were fine with all of this. If you have more changes in elevation via stairs/etc, something with 8" wheels might work better for you.

Finally, it folds for storage. It's still a tad bulky (the front curved handle doesn't collapse), but it does make storage a little easier. It's also not heavy, so tucking it into the car won't be a big issue, either.

Overall, I'm giving this 4 stars. I think it works fine for my needs, and should survive knee surgery (as well as the possible hip surgery the doc keeps mentioning) ...

In the days of COVID... this is how the story begins. Let's set it up. Combine the elements of Work from Home, quiet space at a premium, available enclosed semi-outdoor space, and awesome weather, and you have a situation where the enclosed patio becomes not just ideal for the day-to-day work schedule, but it becomes AWESOME! Only problem is the wifi is on the other end of the property with a solid home construction bulkhead in between along with a sheer wall and other means of interference. I was dropping Zoom meetings, getting late messages, I had a solid 4-5 seconds of speech delay, and my phone would not alert me to anything.

At that point I thought, maybe the router just isn't strong enough. It's only about 40 feet away but still. So I took a chance on a reasonably priced and well-featured (this one) version of a wifi-extender and I am now at full speed. No drops, no lagging, full speed even through a VPN connection. I wasn't sure this was going to be the answer to my speed issues since the base connection isn't terribly fast, but it absolutely worked.

I do need to bring up a quick caveat... the word "extender" may be misleading. The means of extension is by acting as a relay. Thus in order to connect to the home network via the extender, you actually need to connect to the extender instead. If you are prone to moving about the house/property/office, and you need the strongest available connection, you may find that you need to manually switch back and forth to whichever is strongest in the particular location you are at in relation to either the wireless router or the extender. For my purposes this was fine since my work computer stayed put... I just had to switch wifi networks on my phone when I worked in that location.

Everything looked like it was working, but it would not go on the internet correctly. After some troubleshooting and nothing seemed to make sense I swapped the cable and it worked great. I'm now getting close to 40Mbps, and the wifi extender (brand new) was only getting around 18Mbps (not to mention it was broadcasting 2 more access points to all the neighbors). Highly recommend setting up your home network and set your router/modem to not broadcast the SSID (local network name). Even though you use encryption, this can be broken so the better solution is not to publicize the SSID at all. So don't become a victim of Cyber crime, change the default name to something you'll remember and turn that off (it's not that hard if you look that up or call tech support).

To the Seller:> You'll do well to check into quality control for your Ethernet cables.

I received these as a gift for my 58x Jubilee headphones; the stock pads were wearing out, and I was interested in trying something different to replace them. I've ended up loving these, but not without some caveats. Comfort is much improved; the 58x is already considered a comfortable headphone, but I wear glasses, and I found the stock pads exerted too much pressure which quickly made them uncomfortable for me. These pads have remedied the comfort issues handily.
Hobbyists warn against using 3rd party pads with this series of headphones, and with good reason: they change the sound dramatically. To be fair, the change seems very much in line with what the frequency response graphs on the product page indicate, so it's not surprising. But it's still a VERY large increase in bass response, and for the 58x, at least, rather too much; it makes music sound boomy and unclear, and on its own, I think it would probably prevent me from using them. Some of this is down to personal preference, to be sure, but in any event, be prepared for a dramatic change.
I use my headphones on my computer, where I am able to use an EQ to account for this change, and with that done I feel I'm getting the best of both worlds: much improved comfort and sound on par with the original pads. If your setup is similar (or you're looking for a BIG bass boost), these can be a great option; just be ready for the impact they'll have on your audio.

I installed the card into my lovely girlfriend's SFF PC, as an early gift. It was very easy to swap the regular plate with the included low-profile plate, with just a small Phillips screwdriver and a pair of needle-nose pliers. The card seated very easily, and all of the cables plugged in with a very secure click. The system booted up without any problems, and Windows 7 Home Premium 64-bit recognized it almost immediately. It installed the basic drivers, and the everything worked well. Then I made the mistake of installing the latest utility from MSI... After installing, it notified me that there were new final release drivers. I allowed it to install new drivers, and it BSODed Windows.

After the BSOD, I was unable to boot into Windows 7 (the glowing windows icon would freeze), unable to boot into Safe Mode (it would hang up while loading), Last Known Good would boot past the logo before BSODing again, and the repair console was unable to fix the problem - before and after I removed the card. Every time I rolled back to a new restore point before the drivers, it would still freeze. Every utility I used confirmed nothing else was wrong with her system (HDD, memory, mobo, etc).

After a pow-wow with another IT friend, I booted from an Ubuntu CD and was able to access the HDD, and manually removed the MSI utility, driver, and all instances written in the registry. From there, I was finally able to boot into Windows 7. I rolled back to a restore point before I installed the driver, and the system seems to be in good working order again.

For now, I'm running the system without the card. I will attempt to install the card again, after I do a full backup of the system. From what I can tell, there was nothing wrong with the hardware. This seemed like it was entirely the fault of the latest drivers. Once I reinstall the card, and - goodness willing - get to test its performance, I'll re-review the card. Until then, I'm not particularly happy about my purchase.

~~~ UPDATE (December 28, 2014): Third time is apparently the charm. After another failed attempt to install and use the card, I made sure to wipe out every single file written by the graphics utility. I was able to easily revert back to a manual Windows Restore Point I had made, unlike last time. Finally, I re-inserted the card, booted into Windows 7 Home Premium 64-bit, and allowed Windows Update to add the drivers. After restarting, everything appears to work well. Video is VERY crisp. I did some quick benchmarking, and I received a noticeable boost in graphics performance after the upgrade. As such, I am raising my review from 1 star to 3 stars. I will continue to evaluate the performance of the card, and update my review as needed.

In some reviews I read they said you have to let the watch sit overnight before you can wear it... not quite accurate. Per the installation video the adhesive starts to set after about 8 minutes. After 8 minutes, smooth out the edges and they will stay down. I let the adhesive set another 8 minutes and it was good to go. It wasn't going to move.

Here's where people get confused... dry time vs time to fully cure. It only takes about 8 minutes for the adhesive to be mostly dry where you would smooth out any bubbles and edges. After a few more minutes the screen protector is fully adhered to the watch face and you can wear it again.

The video telling you to let the watch dry overnight is talking about total cure time. Which just means the time it takes for the adhesive to come to its full adhesion power.

It's made of hardwood, with multiple lengths of wood securely glued together -- sort of like a butcher block. There are some visible joins in these lengths of wood -- if you're not too picky about this, it's just fine. Likewise, there are some joins in some of the legs. Both desks I ordered had joins in two of the legs, and no joins in the other two. So I put the better legs on the front. But I don't want to give you the idea that these joins are very bad, and they don't affect the strength of the desk. The desk when it's all assembled is really very nice.

The keyboard drawer is much higher quality than I expected. It's also very nice, and at just the right height. There's a moderate odor coming from the finish when first unpacked, but this has dissipated after a day. All in all, I couldn't be happier, and I would rate this 6 stars if that were possible.

I have mixed feelings about this trash can. The thrifty, practical part of me wants to tell you to save your money and buy a $20 plastic can with a swinging lid. The rest of me is more appreciative of comfort, even in something so humble as a trash receptacle.
The TapCan has a clean, simple design that should blend in with many types of decor. Nobody wants to call attention to their trash, after all. The stainless steel on the body of the can is real metal. The lid is just a plastic faux stainless.
The can is sensitive to the lightest tap, so this might be a good option for an elderly or disabled person. It can be operated with a cane or stick. I like the fact that it is silent too- no clanging interruption if you are speaking on the phone! The charcoal pack does appear to help with odors, though I am not sure how often it might need to be replaced, or how easy it is to find the replacement filters. I am sure amazon must have them- they have EVERYTHING! In a pinch I suppose you could buy charcoal meant for a fishtank and use that.
As trashcans go, this is an attractive and non-obtrusive option that has some cool features. You can tuck the bag around plastic holders inside the can to secure it, without any of the bag showing on the exterior. The effortless tap is a big plus also.

I will admit up front that I'm not an audiophile, but I aspire to be one. Either way, I really love great sounding music. I agree with most of the reviews listed, so I won't go into all the details, but here are my thoughts on the V-Moda M-80's.

Originally I was going to get the Senn HD 25 II cans. Everyone raves about the sound quality and I was sold. The only thing I didn't like about the Senn's was the looks. They are not exactly great looking cans. While browsing headfi, I noticed the M-80's were getting a lot of attention and people were comparing them to the HD 25's. With the fact that they actually look great, I decided to pick up a pair.

The build quality on these things are amazing. The flex steel makes it so the headband can flex out to any size and not affect the shape. The cables are awesome. A lot of people have complained about the cloth covered Kevlar cables, but I've not had any problem with them. The biggest complaint was with using the mic on the cable. As the cloth rubs on your clothes people could hear the reverberation. V-Moda now includes a shirt clip to help alleviate this problem. I've yet to use the clip and haven't really had any problems. I don't move around much when using these on the phone though.

The sound quality is simply amazing. As everyone else has said, the bass is tight and right on. I had a couple pairs of Klipsch In-Ear phones (X10 & S4i) and some Sony MDR-V700's that didn't sound this good. The mids and highs sound really nice to me as well, but as I mentioned before, I'm no audiophile.

Comfort wise, these cans are great. With my Sony's, your ears would get hot after about an hour and start hurting after 2 hours. I've listened to these M-80's for 8+ hours straight and never had any discomfort. The memory foam on the headphones conforms to your ears. The longer you listen the better it conforms. I'd say I have an average sized head. If you have a large head you might feel some discomfort, but a quick bend of the headband would likely fix that problem.

The sound isolation is another thing I was concerned about. With the Klipsh in-ear and the Sony circumaural headphones sound isolation was really great. You couldn't hear anything around you. With these headphones being supra-aural I was afraid they would let sound leak in. I was pleasantly surprised how well these isolate sound. I've yet to try them in a very loud environment, they work very well at blocking out noise in normal environments.

The warranty is the last thing that sold me on this set. Not many people have pointed out the amazing warranty that comes with these cans. To start, you get a 2 year warranty against any defects. That's much longer than most company's offer. Due to the fact that these are built like a tank, V-Moda probably feels safe giving that warranty. In addition to the amazing 2 year warranty, it comes with "Immortal Life Program" which provides you with a 50% off coupon should **ANYTHING** happen to them after the 2 year warranty is up.

Overall, I'm incredibly happy with the V-Moda M-80's. I'd highly recommend them to anyone who enjoys high quality sound, likes good looking cans and amazing build quality.

I've had two different K machines die just outside of the warranty period, and in the search of yet another replacement, stumbled upon several varieties of "manual pump"-type gizmos. I've been using another one, but decided to give this one a try since it's smaller and could pack nicely for vacation.

Bottom line: It's easy to use and puts out a respectable cup of coffee.

What I like:
-- small size -- it breaks down into 4 pieces (k-cup holder, water reservoir, rubber pump, and pump cap), so easy to store and pack
-- simple to use -- put k-cup in holder, screw on water reservoir, add water, put pump cap into rubber pump, put pump into water reservoire, pump
-- coffee produced is quite good, maybe not as good as a K machine, but still much better than I expected and definitely drinkable
-- easy to maintain -- clean and dry after use (NO DISHWASHER)

What I don't like:
-- getting the pump into the reservoir filled with hot water is a tad tricky - you have to be VERY careful and steady. There's a sturdy plastic ring in the bottom flange of the pump, so I usually just push on that (gently) until the pump is firmly in place.
-- there's always a little water left in the reservoir after filling because the opening in the bottom of the reservoir is raised slightly. I'm never quite sure whether or not I've pumped all the water out, although usually, I'll see a lot of steam as I pump air. Just something to be aware of.

I've been using it daily now for two weeks and I've had no real issues other than a slight learning curve.

Some things I've learned:
-- do NOT use boiling water with this. As with at least one other version of the same idea, boiling water (as in rolling boil) can cause the plastic to crack. This may be less of a risk with this model because the bottom of the reservoir is plastic, not metal (the others seem to crack because the metal puncture pin expands with the heat), but still -- the user manual says not to use boiling water and I suspect they have a reason. I have an electric kettle that has an adjustable thermostat so I set it so that it shuts off just before reaching a solid boil (got it on Amazon, and it was surprisingly inexpensive). I'm hoping this will add to a longer lifespan for this.
-- don't push too hard on the pump. All that does is force the water through faster and you'll end up with weak coffee (speaking from experience). Take a little time, using gentle pressure just to keep the water flowing.
-- I fill water to the 8-oz line in the reservoir. It usually takes 3-4 "pumps" to get all the water into the cup, occasionally more. I have a 20-oz mug, so I run the process twice with 2 k-cups to get an almost-full mug.

Overall, I really do like this. I'm planning to take it along on my next vacation since the coffee provided in hotel rooms is usually not that good and as long as I can get hot water, I know this will provide a drinkable cup of coffee. Solid 4 stars -- I like it!

First the review:

Great screen protector. S-Pen works just as well as without the protector. Doesn't collect dusts and cleans easily. Once it sets, if you didn't look at the cut-out, you won't be able to tell a protector is on the screen. Highly recommend.

Only problem is that the installation instructions are lame. My wife and I both have Note 8s. I did mine 2x to work out the bugs of installing so I'd get it right for hers. Here's what I did to get a perfect, bubble-free install.

Installation:

1. Wipe the screen down with the provided microfiber cloth
2. Use the included lint remover
3. Wipe with included alcohol swab
4. (Optional) After alcohol evaporates, wipe screen again with mico-fiber cloth
5. Partially separate protector from sheet. Do this from the edge that will line up with the bottom of the phone. Only expose enough to start the process. Recommend using the squeegee to pull it away. DON'T USE YOUR FINGERS EVEN IF YOU WASHED YOUR HANDS!
6. Line up the exposed portion of the protector with the bottom edge of the phone.
7. IMPORTANT: Use the WIDE edge of the squeegee and smooth out the protector. If bubbles appear, gently lift that section and smooth out with the wide edge of the squeegee.
8. Don't attempt to smooth out the edges until the flat part of the screen is smooth. Then use the squeegee to smooth the edges.
9. If you're using a case, wait 15 minutes or so to let the glue set before putting phone in case.

If you look closely and in the right lighting, you'll see "grooves" where you used the squeegee immediately after installation. This is normal. Once the glue on the protector sets, you won't even know there's a screen protector on the phone. It will look just like an unprotected display.

This is a very good cover/protector for the big Note 3 phone. I'm comparing it to the Fintie Samsung Galaxy Note 3 Guardian Series Case (I ordered both), which is only $4.99, whereas this i-Blason is $19.99. I'm rating the silicon/rubber and plastic snap-cover and protector only, not the belt clip. The fit of this more expensive i-Blazon is less snug than the cheaper Fintie. The lip around the glass edges of the phone front kind of rolls away under your fingers with normal use, but the plastic snap-on cover keeps the whole thing secure. It doesn't peel off. However, one big advantage of the softer material in the i-Blason is it is a bit sticky in your hand. This is important for the wide, unwieldy Note 3. For 1-handed use, the extra grip helps. The material of the $4.99 Fintie is stiffer, snugger, but comparatively slick. Both covers would help protect the phone from a drop, but I think the tacky feel of the i-Blason might make it less likely you'd drop it trying to dial or swipe with one hand. Kick stands are very similar and are a must-have if you like to check email, surf or watch videos while eating lunch.
Regarding the belt clips, both the i-Blason and Fintie have a kind of normal, run-of-the-mill cheap swivel clip. I've stopped using belt clip holsters because I work in an industrial facility. Even with my previous Razr Maxx the holster tended to catch on things as I'd walk past. But even normal office furniture, door handles or seat belts can be a danger. Either of these swivel clips would likely snap off under any kind of stress and fling your phone with more force than a normal drop. So I would recommend not putting your big $700 phone in a swivel holster at all. But if it's your thing, please spend the money on the Sedio SURFACE. For me the Sedio is not worth the money ($27.94) just for the silicon/rubber wrapper (although it is the best one...snug, perfect fit, but no more protection than the two described here). But if you must have a swivel clip and holster, the $54.95 Sedio is in a whole different category of strength, security and quality construction. Worth the money given the expense of replacing this top-shelf phone.

Unfortnately there there are two remaining problems that are making me now decide to look for another camera:

1. Echos: When using this camera, is it causes an echo on videoconferencing that others can hear. I cannot hear it. It is so annoying to others that immediately people start talking about it and asking if the call can be done using some other audio. It definitely happens on Microsoft Teams calls as others have said in the Questions section for this product on Amazon. I can't remember if it happened on Webex videocalls also. Others have said switching the audio source solves that problem.

2. Wide View: This may be standard on these cameras. I'll find out when I shop for a new one, but the view is much wider than my native laptop camera. I can't find any way on the camera to "crop" it so that it shows only the person during videoconference and not a lot of what is to the right and left of the person. I solved that problem by installing OBS Studio and the OBS virtual camera. OBS allows me to crop the picture and then uses that video as the "camera" in Microsoft Teams. That works very well to get a good cropped video, however, the image quality went way down and it freezes up sometimes, so it is not a great solution because I end up not having smooth starts to videoconferences with all the troubleshooting I have to do to get OBS, the webcam, and the conferecing software to all work together.

This is a very technical post, if you're in to that stuff, read on. To summarize for everyone else, this product no longer works on Linux. Older revisions of this product did. It is with great sadness that I write to say this product no longer works with Linux. The version shipped to me used the MT7610u MediaTek chipset. After much digging and hair pulling I was only able to get this slightly working (very buggy and unstable) using the driver found on Github, in repository ulli-kroll/mt7610u. Of the handful of drivers I tried, this is the only drive I could find that would actually compile, the rest are broken. NetworkManager locks and caused the whole system to panic and freeze when the driver is loaded. Stopping NetworkManager first allowed the driver to load without the system crashing and I was able to connect to my network. The card was extremely unstable. I was able to send about 3-5 ICMP packets before the connection would drop and re-establish a few moments later. It looks like the driver author is currently working on it so it uses mac80211 so maybe there is hope for this to work at some point in the future.

First things first -- before using ANY over-the-counter meds, including this one, check with your doctor to make sure it won't interfere with any other meds you're taking or negatively impact any specific conditions you might have. Diphenhydramine has been used for years as an antihistamine -- it just happens to also work nicely as a sleep aid.

Now -- let's talk specifically about this product. Each tablet contains 50mg of the medication, which is double the strength of most diphenhydramine products. I have taken diphenhydramine for several years under the guidance of my doctors (including my pulmonary doctor -- I have stage 3 COPD, and there's always a concern with meds that can negatively impact my breathing) -- not every night; just when I know I'm going to have problems drifting off, and my doctors all recommended taking 50mg. This product means I have to take only 1 pill instead of two, and this one is a soft gel which means it dissolves more quickly.

What I like most about diphenhydramine as opposed to other sleep aids is that I don't feel foggy or "spacey" when I wake up in the morning. I probably use it once or twice a week on average (no more than that), and only when I feel the need. It works fairly quickly for me, and I drift off within 20 minutes or so. And I stay asleep until morning.

This doesn't work for everyone -- one of my brothers has tried it and it had no effect at all. But for me, it can mean tht difference between an uncomfortable night waking up tired, and a night where I get to sleep quickly and awaken rested and ready to go. Solid 4 stars -- I like it.

Got this for my 20-something daughter at Verizon store very early in July. She still loves, loves, loves it and would give it 5 stars. However, her data usage went from under 2 gigs to over 7 the first month she used it because of default settings allowing so many apps to run in the background, and because of the phone's reluctance to connect to anything less than optimal, super-perfect wi-fi signals. Correcting this has been easy with a bit of attention and vigilance, and luckily we had increased our family data plan to 8G (rather than scaling back to 4G, as the salesperson said we might based on our historical usage) and had 8G of rollover data (now lost - you can only carry over data for one month with Verizon) that would have protected us last month even if my daughter had actually streamed video and actually used much real data (as opposed to background apps). So all is well -- I will continue to watch reviews and may even consider purchasing this phone when I tire of my old Motorola Droid Maxx. But buyer beware: DO read the instructions and take care about what is running in the background, and about setting data alerts and limits even if you think you don't need them (unless you have unlimited data ... then none of this is an issue).

I tried one of the less expensive cover/keyboard and returned it for several reasons. I kept this one, but just barely.

The Good:

The App that you can optionally install seems to work very well also. The keyboard is well laid out and the keys give good feedback when typing.
