The Bad:

This thing will exactly double the weight of your device. You don't realize what a difference that makes until you put them together. You go from 1 to 2 pounds.

This part is not Logitech's fault, but the Galaxy Tab 3 has the charging port on the bottom but should be coming out of the side. If you add this Samsung design defect to this cover, it means you can not charge and use the device at the same time when propped up on the stand. That is completely ridiculous!

The Ugly:

You can not charge the device with the cover closed (tablet protected) because Logitech didn't put a hole in the cover. This inexcusable design flaw can be overcome with a steady hand and an X-Acto knife. I created a square hole in the cover to accommodate the charger. It takes a lot of lining up, but mine came out perfectly.

When using certain charging cables, the plastic the tablet snaps into stops the cable from going into the tablet all the way. This second design flaw from Logitech can be corrected with a steady had and a dremmel tool to remove some of the plastic that sticks out over the charging port.

On the other end of the cover/keyboard the plastic that holds the tablet in covers half of the IR emitter. So if you want to use your device as a TV remote, it has to be held just right.

The worst part of this device is that if you flip the cover/keyboard open 180 degrees, half the time you can't type on the on screen keyboard because the cover/keyboard magnets make the device thinks its closed. Or worse, you unlock it and the two halves touch and it locks and turns off the tablet again. (Yes I know this feature can be turned off on the tablet)

Overall:
I kept the device because it is well made (but not well thought out), I was able to customize it to overcome design flaws, and after I customized it I couldn't return it. Half the problems above wouldn't be an issue of Samsung put the charging port on the side. But I have to assume if Logitech sells a cover/keyboard for this specific device, that should have at least tried it first. GMRS walkie-talkies like this have been around for decades. Unfortunately, the technology hasn't really improved in all that time. The specs that are listed in the description are greatly exaggerated. We only get 4-5 hours of moderate use from the rechargeable batteries. Fortunately, you can replace them with fresh AA batteries in the field to extend your usage time. The 20 mile range is really a hoax. Even the most optimal situation when one of us is on top of a hill and the others are visible in the valley below, we've never gotten more than 10 miles. In clear flat situations like across a lake or a farm field, range is a 3-4 miles at best. In a forest or city where there are lots of obstructions, range can be less than 1 mile.

20 years ago, few people had cell phones so these radios were really popular. Not so much anymore. That means you get much less interference on each channel. We find the radios useful for family outings since the kids don't have cell phones and many of the parks we visit have terrible cell phone coverage.

The radios are fairly lightweight (about 6 ounces each including the batteries). The package includes 3 battery packs and 2 chargers. One of the chargers has a splitter so it can charge 2 radios at the same time. You can also use your micro-USB cell phone charger to charge the radios. You can also use your own rechargeable AA batteries with your own charger. Replacing the batteries is kind of a hassle since the belt clip blocks the battery cover, though I suppose that also helps keep the battery cover in place. No carrying cases or storage case is included, through the radios are pretty durable and the shipping box works well for storage.

Note that USA use requires a Federal FCC radio license. The photo here is from the instruction manual. Many (perhaps most) users violate Federal law and use them without license, but who knows what enforcement will be like in the future. Other countries have stricter laws and I have heard about some tourists getting into trouble using radios like this.

I bought this keyboard to replace the non-wave, non-ergonometric keyboard that came with my HP desktop. I have used similar Logitech keyboards in the past and have been using a Logitech optical mouse with the HP keyboard. When I saw this product, which ships a mouse with the keyboard, I was please to purchase it.

The keyboard is full-size. It is embedded in a case that is deeper than the HP because it includes a wider, more comfortable wrist rest. This is covered in a pleasantly tactile dimpled material and works very well for me--with somewhat small hands for a man. The ergonometrics include a qwerty keyboard where the keys are set in a wave of changes in elevation to reflect the longer length of one's middle finger while providing for the reaching distance between lines of keys. There is a moderate arc to the set of the keys that is not as extreme as the true ergo board, which is more of a vee-shape. Keys operate with a springy, positive action, requiring a definite touch and not being too sensitive. The result is a board that is easy and comfortable to use, as I do, for serious spells of writing. There are twelve programmable function keys and clear instructions for setting them up plus buttons for 'insert', 'print screen', pause/break and rocking controls to zoom in and out on pages. The top edge of the board has a tilted panel with sound and track controls and is optimized to work with Windows Media Center. A single button brings up a calculator. There are other buttons I am less likely to use and have not investigated. One of them brings up Windows desktop gadgets or settings and another opens Windows Photo Gallery. A large button off the keyboard near the shift and control keys permits application switching for users having 'SetPoint' software.

I have always liked Logitech's optical mouse. They have improved its wireless transmitter, making it a small, rectangular plug-in module, that takes up next to no room on a desk or work table; transmits signals very well and stays out of the way. My earlier version was embedded in a round case about three inches in diameter and got in the way from time to time. Logitech calls this new device a 'Unifying Receiver' and explains it a bit on page 14 of the Operator's Manual. Basically, this is a plug-in and forget it type of device. The mouse is made of quality materials and feels good in the hand.

I've tried out 3 different cases for the iPad Pro 11-inch to date and this is the best one in the bunch. It's still lacking in certain ways, and I'm holding out hope that someone will figure out the problems and come up with the perfect case. Until then, this is my winner-ish.

So, this one does a few things very well.

1. It has a hard-ish case that will protect your iPad from moderate drops on a hard surface with one caveat. You cover needs to be closed to protect the screen. Otherwise, the screen could still hit a hard surface and crack. I'm not saying it will protect your screen 100% with the cover closed, but that it does offer better protection than if you have it open.

2. It does a semi-decent job as performing as a stand while using your iPad in landscape mode. But even then, there are still issues with the angle. It still doesn't have a great angle for using FaceTime -- it doesn't raise up the iPad enough, so you either have to tilt it forward or use another stand. But for just using it with other apps, it has multiple angles that each work well enough.

The stuff that doesn't work yet is the support for portrait mode. There's really no way to get this cover to work with portrait mode with any degree of stability. You can kind of open the cover and use it like an "L"-shape to make portrait mode if all you need is exactly 90° vertical. Even then, it's still going to be semi-unstable.

The pencil holder could also use some work, but it does a good job of storing the pencil while still being able to charge the pencil. The only issue is getting the pencil out of the case is a little wonky because you pretty much have to push it out from the back until you can grab it from the front. If you have big fingers like me, it's a little tough to push it out the smallish hole in the back. Luckily, the case is a bit flexible, so my big fingers can manage to shove it out. Not perfect, but passable.

Overall, I like this case for the hardness and the overall protection it will afford from drops, but I always pair this with a padded slip-cover style case to have an extra level of protection. This case by itself might prevent a cracked screen if it fell out of your backpack while walking on a soft surface, but I wouldn't trust it to fall on a sidewalk without taking some damage. With this cover inside a padded slip-cover case, your chances are way better and you'd probably be okay with a short fall.

That said, this case is of very good quality material and the magnets are fairly strong (but they could be a bit stronger). It turns off the screen when you close the cover which is how it's supposed to work (some covers don't). And it will charge your pencil when it's stored.

Now if it just had better angles and a portrait mode with also-better angles this could be a five-star product.

For now, it's the best that I've tried, but still only 4-stars.

4 cubes butter, softened
2 heaping cups dark brown sugar (packed, then heap that shiz)
½ cups white sugar
2 tablespoons vanilla
1 ½ teaspoon salt
1 ½ teaspoons baking soda
3 eggs
6 cups flour

You get a metal jar with 60 Capsules of Cordyceps mushroom powder. Each capsule contains 500mg of hot water extracted Cordyceps mushroom powder. It tastes and looks as expected. I open capsules and pour the powder into my green drink, and these are easy to open. Too easy, as it turns out. If you leave the capsules in the jar until the moment you take it out to use it, everything is fine. However, the capsules are not airtight and are affected by humidity. I set two of these out on my napkin intending to eat them at lunch, several hours away. By then, on a humid day, the mushroom powder in the capsules had hardened into a smaller pellet. It was still edible. I decided to have the second one until supper, another four hours in humid weather, and the mushroom powder was both hard and gooey by then. I didn't think it was safe to eat, so I threw it away. So it is a fine supplement, but don't leave it out in humid air. I appreciate that this product is non-GMO.

The Aiyima is overhyped. It's not a "giant killer". Its sound is pretty nice, but it clips too often. It clips into my desktop speakers, and it even clips using it as a preamp into another amplifier. Since clipping can damage the speakers, this makes the Aiyima essentialy unusable for me.

If you're not famliar with what clipping sounds like, it's a sort of crinkly distortion that almost sounds like your midrange woofer might be broken or coming detached. It happens when your unit is overworked and can't produce the full audio sine waves.

Clipping is especially disappointing since Aiyima rates the amp as 100 W or whatever, which is clearly false. My 30W desktop amp has never clipped with this system, but then it's from a reputable vendor, Denon.

I wanted to like this amp, but clipping is a dealkiller since it can damage the speakers. Not worth the risk unless your speakers are so cheap you don't care.

I have used this on four computers so far, Windows XP and Windows 7. The NETGEAR WN111 outperforms both of them. My experience with the WNDA3100 is that is continually drops the connection. While connected it works well, but too many drops! On two side-by-side computers, on the 2nd floor of a building (router on 1st) the NETGEAR WN111 was consistently operating at 3-4 times the speed of the AirLink101. I have bought all of my NETGEAR WN111's for less than $10 a piece, refurbished. They have all worked. There are specific drivers that must be used in US, and also for XP and Win7. These are WN111v2_NA_SW2.0_setup or an older version wn111_setup_21_na (NA stands for North America) and a special Windows 7 version wn111v2_3.0_setup_win_7. These are easily found at NETGEAR and other sites. The program DriveMax recently found an update for one of these. I did not note the version of it. I am sure it can be easily found. I did notice an improvement in performance.

I googled the malfunction and found out that the drive had no partitions.

So first step was to get in Disk Management, find the drive, click on the 113+gb unallocated space and create a partition.

Step two, reboot and change my boot sequence because Samsung Magician felt it was necessary to change it for me and made this new SSD my boot drive, even though it had no OS on it to boot.

Step three, change my power management plan back to what I had before because Samsung Magician felt it was better to change it to hibernate instead of what I wanted. I hate Hibernate.

After that it worked great. I use this SSD for games only because it's so damn fast, but I wish the included software and instructions were better, hence the 4 stars and not 5.

I was skeptical but went ahead and ordered this signal booster. After receiving I plugged it in, in my basement home office, with the antennae inside an exterior window. The window is not even on the side of the house facing the cell tower. I then placed my Blackberry into the cradle and nearly immediately the signal went from none or one bar to 3 or 4 bars! I then tested with my Samsung i920 and it too went to four bars from only one. Both use Verizon by the way.
AUTO
Just this past weekend I brought the booster along in my car to a spot where Calls have always dropped. Even in this dead zone the booster helped enough to retain signal and allow a call to be placed. I also used the i920 as a hotspot for my iPad 2 in the parking lot of our daughter's dance class, which normally has low signal and only 1X service. But with the booster the service went to EV/3G and the data rates increased significantly.
I may order a second one to leave in the car.
Additional notes:
- Given how good it works I do not plan to keep the cradle close to my head, but overall we are very happy with the performance and value of this product.
- For my office I was able to use an extension cable, previously used for a WiFi router, to move the antennae to the best location I could find, while keeping the cradle and cell phone within reaching distance. I also tried it with an old WiFi antennae - one of the longer ones (~12") designed to boost wireless signals - and that may have yielded a slight increase, but I have no way to accurately measure.
- It does use peak USB voltage with consistency so I would not recommend the use of a laptop or PC USB port for continuous power (this usually causes a Windows machine to use much higher CPU). Plugging the USB power cable into a USB wall plug works just fine. I also plug that wall plug into a timer so that the booster is only on during the day when it is needed.

Neem really helps with my itchy scalp (I add it to my Castile liquid soap which is also my shampoo) and mix it with carrier oil or use straight to soothe my eczema. It's also a great insecticide. I'm baffled by some of the bad reviews I've read. It would appear that many people buy neem not knowing much if anything at all about it, then are surprised or blame the product rather than their own ignorance. So to those reviewers, spoiler alert: 1) Neem oil won't and shouldn't smell like roses LOL! It's aroma is rather pungent...think of a marriage between garlic and sulfur only more gentle. If it doesn't smell pungent, it ain't the real McCoy; 2) It should be solid at room temperature unless you live in a very hot climate. Just put it in a cup of very hot water (remember to remove the cap), and let it sit for a few minutes. It will liquefy. You can then use it directly, add it to your shampoo, moisturizer, carrier oil, or insect spray bottle. If you live in a cool place and it's liquid, beware, unless you keep your house like a sauna; 3) Neem oil, I'm told, comes in a variety of shades depending on where it's grown. It can range from golden to a very deep brown. I've only used the lighter variety. My one and only experience with a very dark "neem" oil turned out to not be neem as it remained liquid at 50 degrees. But I don't think the color was the issue. Lastly, neem is not the only safe and natural insecticide. You can use a water/alcohol spray or make insecticidal soap (1 tablespoon oil, 1 teaspoon castile soap to 1 quart water....adding a little garlic and chili pepper is a plus...and repeat every few days to get eggs). Soothing skin/scalp options also include aloe vera, shea butter, cucumber and many others. Happy hunting!

Close to the router, I measured download speed at 178 mbps and upload speed at 24 mbps. I walked outside 100 feet from the downstairs beacon and measured the download speed at 45 mbps and the upload speed at 18 mbps. My iPhone showed connection another 100 feet away as long as I had line of sight to the front door but speedtest wouldn't take a measure that far away. My old wireless network was substantially slower.

Alexa would break up on the old network but is playing steady now.

Day 2: The main eero is running hot but not the beacon. I also realized the lack of a second ethernet port means I can't plug in my ooma. The one port runs directly to my iMac.

After a week, still working great. No downtime or lagging. Still running really hot but I'll use that to my advantage during the winter. I had a houseful of guests this weekend and no one complained about poor connections like they did with the old setup. Unexpected and almost irrelevant but I really like the nightlight feature in the beacon.

I bought this keyboard to replace an aging Microsoft ergonomic keyboard. I've always loved the comfort of the ergonomic keyboards from Microsoft but their durability is unimpressive. I've had two of the things killed by a few DROPS of water, whereas some $10 keyboards have survived entire glasses of soda or coffee being spilled on them. That's infuriating when you've spent $50-$70 on a keyboard, which is quite a lot to pay for a fragile rubber dome and membrane device without much by way of programming features.

Which is why I'm switching (pun intended) to a mechanical keyboard!

I'm reviewing the Z-88 keyboard with the Brown switches today. This keyboard comes in two versions: Blue switches with an audible click, and Brown switches with a noise level similar to a rubber dome keyboard. I might have gone with the Blue version as the action is meant to be more crisp but I've not bought this keyboard for gaming. I have a separate Logitech one-handed mini gaming keyboard for that.

The small form factor of this keyboard, especially without the numerical keypad, was attractive as I like to keep the keyboard on my desk and not in a keyboard tray. To get a keyboard this small means sacrificing on the ergonomics though.

I've found this keyboard to be incredibly uncomfortable to type on without wrist support. It's my fault for not ordering a wrist pad for this device, as I should have known that holding my arms up in the proper position while typing would be both tiring and irritating. A rolled up t-shirt is doing the trick at present. With wrist support this keyboard is perfectly usable. It's a bit cramped for typing but I'm not going to dock points for that. I wanted a keyboard that was at most only slightly larger than a portable Bluetooth keyboard and that's what I got.

The Brown switches lack any sort of feedback for when you've pressed down far enough for the switch to engage. You'll know when the switch bottoms out. The action has a nice amount of resistance so the keystrokes don't feel sloppy. The keys do wobble a bit but don't feel flimsy. I'm not sure if it's the switch mechanism or the way the keycap rides the switch. The spacebar has a nice mechanical spring feel to it. It would be nice if the Enter key had the same spring loaded feel but it feels like any other key.

Caps Lock key illuminates brighter when engaged, as does the Scroll Lock which is a function of the Page Down key. Nice touch.

All of the backlight features are programmable from the keyboard. One less app on my computer to program an input device. I like the one that lights up the key after you press it. Steady backlight or the mode that pulses slowly are nice for low light.

How many other keyboards have LED backlit mechanical switches for less than $50? A great value for the price even if you do have to spend another $15 on a wrist cushion.

We'll see how it holds up to a cup of coffee being spilled on it later.

The Good: 1. Super easy to set up. It paired with my iPhone5 in less than 5 seconds. I didn't even have to enter the Bluetooth code on the phone. 2. Easy to play your music - simply press the "Music" button and you're off and playing whatever playlist you have set up on the phone; no need to even touch the phone unless you want to change your playlist or look for a specific song. 3. Voice commands work well.

The Bad: 1. No display to help with the setup. Everything is by voice prompts and I could not find a way to adjust the volume for the setup - the commands and prompts blare out at full volume that can be heard for a block in every direction. 2. Itty Bitty status lights mounted on the side where they are impossible to see without removing the device from the visor. 2. Loud, shrill "PING" when you turn it off that will make you wince every time; you'll never get used to it. 3. When talking on the phone, unless you speak up you'll be hearing a lot of "are you still there?" or, simply, "hello?, hello?". The people on the other end will tell you that it sounds like you're on the speakerphone (well, I guess that technically you are). Also, your voice comes through to them "echo-ey". For short conversations only; if you conduct a lot of business over your phone or otherwise make a lot of longer calls, go with one of those "Mr. Spock" things for your ear. 4. I've seen complaints in here from others about the caller ID; mine works OK with my iPhone, but will only announce names that are in my contact list. Otherwise, it simply recites the incoming phone number. And, it takes so long for this thing to announce that your caller will probably have decided you aren't answering and will have hung up by the time it's through. 5. Limited FM frequencies; it won't go below 89.9, but I understand that may be an FCC thing so I'll give Motorola the benefit of the doubt on this. 6. For you iPhone owners, the advertised "Motospeak" and "Car Finder" apps are available ONLY for Android devices. You'll find this out only AFTER you open the box and remove everything.

and The Ugly: 1. Sound quality through the FM link to your car stereo is pretty bad; and that's being charitable. I was able to improve it a little by trying a few different "unused" FM frequencies. If you're planning on using this to play your beloved classical collection while stuck in traffic, forget it. Listening to an AM radio station will sound better. (For you Ford owners who gave up trying to figure out your Sync system, go back and work with it again. When you can get it functioning, it sounds very nice)

Summary:

Clint Eastwood: Easy to use and set up. Voice commands work pretty good (but speak up!)

Pauley Shore: Terrible FM sound; poor quality phone sound. Apps not available for iPhone.

NOTE: After using this a little longer, I have found it awkward with heavier or longer lenses. You kind of need to use two hands to tighten both knobs at once, and with heavier setups (I'm talking 3-4lbs heavy, not 10lbs heavy), you can't count on a lighter tension to hold things while you tighten both knobs. Also, I've found a glitch developed in one of the tightening knobs where as you're turning it it feels like it hits a bump where it gets tighter for a bit, then looser, then tight again. Not good. I'm probably going to try a different head.

Original Revue:
A Cheap Good Ball Head is a rare animal. Look at the reviews for almost any head <$100 (and most <$300) and you'll see them described as junk, useless, or "maybe I can use this to hold my flash."

Features you would like in your Ball head and how this Bieke/Cowboy head stacks up:
SOLID - won't drift with the weight of your gear (and won't drop your gear!). It holds my medium DSLR (Canon 70D) with 1.5 lb lenses without a hitch. I don't have any bigger than that... I just calibrated my focus and this held the camera rock solid and even held its aim perfectly while I swapped lenses. I also did some macro with it. I'll attach a photo if Amazon lets me.

Easy To Adjust: Ideally you would like to simply turn a knob or lever and have your camera locked in exactly where it was aiming before you tightened. This head doesn't do that. It has two knobs which you will want to tighten together, which can be awkward while aiming the camera. This is the price you pay for a $22 head vs a $300 head. It will stay on target pretty well if you tighten the knobs together - or alternate tightening each a little. This is a bit of a pain. I wouldn't recommend this head if your work requires frequent adjustments. You would probably want a $$$ head. But better to have 2 knobs and have the option of holding the camera's position vs most cheap heads with one knob and the camera is off target once fixed.
Visible Bubble level(s). Yup
Standard Quick release Plate: Nope. Also, what's the deal with having to unscrew a knob to release the quick release? What's the point? You may as well just screw directly into the camera if you're going to have to do that (though that'd be tricky with a ball head). Still, it's kind of lame that way.

But here's the thing: For $22 (or for $50), I don't think you're going to find anything else as good. Probably you're going to go over $100 before you significantly improve on this (and some >$100 are worse).

I also like the pan capability - with lock. Not all ball heads have it and it's pretty convenient. If you just want to change the pan, you don't have to loosen the main head and re-lock. It's tolerably smooth, but I doubt you'll want to use it for video. Maybe in a pinch, but not ideal.

NOTE: this head is sold under many names. I think the dual knob ball lock is fairly distinctive, so that would cue you in. Beike is the actual manufacturer though it's relabled all over the place. Even this Cowboy Studio model, labeled "Afaith" in the Amazon photo said "Beike" on the actual head. As of this writing, this Cowboy Studio version was the cheapest I found.

Durability: It appears solid, but I've only been using it for a week. Threads could strip. Bolts could shear. Time will tell.

I understand that this blanket is an investment - I never would have imagined I would pay so much for a damn blanket - but this is a "must" for people with trouble sleeping/relaxing due to anxiety.

This blanket definitely helps me sleep better through the night. I definitely feel more relaxed when I crawl underneath it and it is covering me from neck to toe.

I did a LOT of research before buying and went with this brand. First, the promo video with the young women made me want to buy it - very relatable. I use this blanket on my bed to sleep at night, so it is always flat, and I don't have an issue with the ties. The weighted blanket doesn't really slide around that much inside the cover, and it is easy to fix. I only had to re-tie the shell to the blanket after a full 2 months of daily use. The weights are reinforced within the patches and I can't foresee anything going wrong with the actual weighted blanket. And the minkies on the shell are incredibly wonderful. When I get anxious I rub my hands over them. I know it sounds weird to anyone who doesn't live with anxiety/panic - it would sound weird to me pre-anxiety too - but the minky texture is SO calming omg. Really a huge plus.

I'm regularly amazed and the kind of sound quality that's available at a low cost these days. I've developed a bit of a habit for cheap IEMs, but in the past I've always associated earbuds (that don't seal with the ear canal) with tinny, middling sound. I got these on a lark, given the cost, and I've been very pleasantly surprised. These are good-- not just "for the price," but on their own, and they've found their way into regular usage for me, even compared to much more expensive headphones and earbuds.

Comfort is a big reason for that: the earbud form factor is light and convenient, making them great for around the house wear. They don't block out external noise, which can be good or bad depending on your use. In terms of sound, I don't want to oversell them--they're $10 headphones--but they're undeniably solid, and for listening to music in the background they provide a nice, balanced sound. They remind me a bit of the Koss KSC75s, another famous value headphone: a little bright and light on bass, but otherwise a better tone than you'll find in significantly more expensive headphones.

The build feels a little cheap, which is understandable since they *are* cheap. Still, I'd be a little concerned about durability if I were lugging them around everywhere. And a caveat: earbuds like these can be very sensitive to positioning; if they sit in your ear a little differently, that can have a significant impact on the sound. For me, though, I've got no complaints. These have punched well above their weight.

I like the case because the case is sleek and matches the color of my phone. There's a few cons that are outlined below that would prevent me from picking up another one of these in the future. That said, I don't consider it a waste of money. The case is functional and works for (most) of what I need it for.

Pros:
The champagne color of the case matches the color of the phone well.
The fit of the case is snug. The phone doesn't wiggle or shift inside the case at all.
The case is easy to remove for cleaning.
The case does not obstruct the USB cable.
**Most** 3.5mm jacks will fit without issue. However, I have a couple that are obstructed by the case due to the adapter itself. It's not necessarily a fault of the case, but you might elect to replace your 3.5mm cord if it doesn't fit well.

Cons:
Biggest con is that it covers the IR blaster entirely. If you want to use it as a remote (which you can do with this phone), you'll have to take off the case to do it. This is contrary to the product description, "Perfect cutouts for the camera, speakers and other ports." I read that to mean it would include the IR port.
I'm a little surprised how many scratches the case has accumulated in a short time. Previous cases I've owned have retained a near flawless look (they seem to have resisted scratches better than this one).
The words on the back of the case are dorky. I'd prefer to have a slick and untouched back (instead of a logo plastered in the corner).

If you want 4K in a 32-inch TV, this is the one to buy. Even if you don't want 4K capability in your 32-inch TV, this is still the one to buy. It's the best 32-inch I've ever had or seen, and it's also superior to Sony's other 32-inch TV, which is only offering 720p max.

I had to deduct a star because of the included remote control. This TV has Google TV with Google Voice Assistant, where you press the microphone button on a remote control and then Google will control the TV for you, including turning it off, and also answer all of your other Google inquiries. The operating system in the TV is fast. Sound is okay, but of course, not as great as some of Sony's larger TVs that push the sound out from all over the screen, as opposed to small speakers at the bottom like this TV has. Of course, you can easily add an external speaker, if desired.

Viewing angles are not nearly as good as Sony's larger 4K 2022 models, but it doesn't bother me since I am almost always just watching the TV straight on.

The price is higher than a lot of inferior 32-inch TVs, but again, the Sony technology offered, along with it capable of 4K, justifies the higher price, in my opinion.

The screen is very easy to read. You select the battery type on the dial. Put one probe onto the positive, one on the negative end of the battery. Now the meter, going up in 5% jumps will tell you what percentage of the battery remains.

The probes have spring-loaded tips with textured ends so they grip the battery you push them against.

Consider the price of these and that hearing is subjective. what sounds good to me may not sound the same to you. keep that in mind and in context of what I say here.

I went to youtube and found a few things to listen to in order to judge the sound quality of these headphones. Music I had been listening to and enjoying for years so I know what its supposed to sound like. I listened to a headphone test, played some online games, ASMR, and watched movies.

For music, they sound pretty good. They are not high end or audiophile in any way, but they give a fullness and range that's better than I expected. They dont have low end like a subwoofer but the bass is meaty enough to be satisfying.

The headphone test I listened to had a sweep of frequencies, leaving the listener to mark the number at which they begin hearing and stop hearing tones. I scored these at around 30 - 120,000 (very non scientific). the series of tests in the video left me satisfied with the results. I feel these would probably rate somewhere in the "upper middle" of headphones tested against the video. in my subjective opinion I would say they did very well.

watching movies is where these get interesting. the separation is very good. simulated surround works very well. they do not sound like my actual movie sound system with the subwoofer, BUT! they work well enough that I can watch with the volume a bit loud and its satisfying. I did notice that I could still detect the projector fan running so I am not sure how noise cancelling these actually are. The foam cups feel nice for a while but after prolonged use, the length of a movie... they hurt my ears. I find that if I change position after a while it helps a lot.

Gaming is pretty good as well. good sound quality, nice separation, audio cues are accurate enough to be able to find team mates or enemies based on sound position. the MIC seems to be pretty ok as well. my voice is fairly deep and carries easily. no issues on the MIC picking me up for my friends to hear me clearly.

ASMR is where I *really* like these. I tested these against a few different ASMR channels on youtube. Some are better than others depending on their equipment and techniques BUT! I have found that with the sound UP the whispers and scratches/crinkles sounds they make will trigger the ASMR response. That's tricky to do because the audio needs to trick your body into believing that the sound/voice is actually close enough to your ear to "feel" it. These headphones do very well for that.

notable flaws in these headphones after a few weeks of use -
the pain after prolonged use. I feel that I should be able to sit through a movie without feeling discomfort of pressure against my ears.

the volume / vibration control that's in the cable feels a bit heavy but the heaviness doesn't translate to "quality" in the thumb wheels that control the device. I would like to see something more... "engineered feeling" if I need to have that weight swinging around like that.

overall I would recommend these. they feel rather solid and they sound good enough. for the price I am not sure you could find better. if you need something audiophile quality you would not be looking at gaming headsets anyway, right?

I received a Lenox white pasta bowl for review.

Lenox is famous for beautiful, expensive china and crystal, and this particular line of china is billed by Lenox as, "casual luxe." That term basically means that, in contrast to traditional, delicate china, this china is advertised to be microwave-safe and dishwasher safe in order to provide "easy living convenience."

All these claims are true, and this bowl is lovely. The major issue with this product is its price. If you are quite well off, you might consider it both affordable and desirable to dine off expensive, fancy china like this on an everyday basis. Alternatively, a newly married couple of average means who long to own expensive china might settle for "casual luxe" such as this line of china instead of traditional, much more expensive china.

Some consumers might consider that the expense of this china is mitigated by the fact that Lenox offers a "lifetime breakage guarantee." Unfortunately, this guarantee consists of Lenox merely paying half the cost of what your broken dish is selling for at the moment it breaks. And, of course, you would have to mail it to them at your expense. Those things taken together mean that it would very likely cost the same to outright purchase a replacement dish--if they are currently still making the style you originally purchased.

In short, if you have a plump pocketbook and enjoy beautiful table settings, this lovely china might be exactly what you're looking for.

You need to read the directions on the insert and season this wok properly BEFORE you use it.

Here's a trick, take the heat diffuser cap off of your gas burner (if you have one) so that instead of getting a ring of flames it shots the flame straight up. Not all gas ranges can do this but if yours does you'll get a more centralized, hotter cone of flame which is great for using a wok on a traditional range. I even bought a cast iron wok ring that sits on my range top which cradles the wok so it stay in place while I cook. Helps a lot.

SEASON SEASON SEASON. Wash the wok well to take off any oil from manufacturing. Then heat up the entire work until it changes color everywhere, tilting it around the flame to get it all heated. Then pour in a tablespoon of vegetable oil and using a paper towel held with tongs rub the oil all over then return the wok to the burner and leave it for 5 or so minutes. It will smoke a lot. Clean the oil out and repeat with new oil. Keep doing this 3-4 times to build up a nice seasoning seal.

NOW YOU CAN USE YOUR WOK! This carbon steel wok is FANTASTIC! It is heavy and distributes heat well. The handle may get a little loose when seasoning, just run it under water a few times to expand it back into snugness. This wok is large and can handle a whole lot of food. Very professional, I highly recommend.

If you're trying to decide if this is worth the extra cost compared to the older style filtered water pitchers, it definitely is. I am not a patient person, and I absolutely despise standing over the sink waiting for the water to trickle into the bottom of the old pitcher that filtered between a top and bottom level, excruciatingly slowly, so I could fill it up enough to at least get two water bottles worth before filling it again. In each model I ever had the top level-- pre filtered-- would hold about a quarter as much water as the bottom level, so you'd have to wait for water to filter through the top into the bottom and then refill the top at least 3 times before the bottom was full. I rarely had the patience for that and just wouldn't bother, so I never ended up actually having enough cold filtered water.

This filters the water as you pour it out of the pitcher rather than as you fill up the pitcher, so you can fill it to the top very quickly and easily and always have cold water in the fridge ready to go into a bottle or glass.

It does still have to filter the water, so you're moving the waiting step to when you pour it into a glass or water bottle. It does take less time than the old style pitcher, and most importantly you aren't stuck over the sink waiting for the process to finish.

Even though this costs more than the other type of pitchers it's much more affordable than the type that attaches to the sink. The replacement filters for those are painfully expensive, and personally
I think the water from this style of filter tastes better.

This does have a light on the lid to indicate when the filter needs replacing, which I think is a helpful feature.

One thing I've found is that when there's not much water left in the pitcher it filters much more slowly, so it's helpful to refill it before it's empty to save the frustration. It also took me a couple minutes to
figure out the instructions for how to place the filter, which turned out to be very, very easy when done correctly, so if you're struggling to remove the filter cover you're most likely doing it wrong.

If you weren't aware, dry shampoo is essentially a blowtorch with powder in it. This product doesn't have enough scent to cover up the odor of the butane and propane accelerants, which wafts into the rest of my apartment since my bathroom doesn't have an exhaust fan. Butane and propane are odorless gasses so manufacturers add an unpleasant odor to them so you can detect explosive gases just by smell. I can smell it on myself for hours so I usually put some cologne in my hair to cover it up.

It seems like I have to spray quite a lot to get the powder to come out, and it makes my scalp very dry. The trick is holding your hair up with a brush and spraying into it, rather than spraying directly on your head. That will minimize the scalp dryness.

It gets my hair from oily looking to just shiny. So it looks nice. The texture is mildly unpleasant though. Again, "dry" is the word. Not chalky, just dry. Strangely it feels okay when you first apply it but gets dryer as the day goes on.

I'm sure some of these things are universal to all dry shampoos if you've got really oily hair, but the lack of scent could be improved.

I'll use the rest of this two pack, but sparingly, and probably wont order again.

I got both this and the Braun to compare them. I expected to prefer this one, but found that the Braun is actually better.

Minor comparisons:
This one has great marketing, a beautiful box and instruction booklet, and the product itself feels more premium as a result. Both Braun and this one are easy to understand and use. I haven't used this one long enough to confirm, but based on my good results with Braun and the similarities with this one, they both effectively remove hair (as a pale person with dark hairs). This one has a bigger ventilator to cool faster, and is less sensitive to the light sensor being perfectly aligned so it's slightly easier to with the larger head on places like ankles (though this may come with an eye safety risk). I can't speak too badly of it and think it's still worth buying.

Major comparison:
The 2 main differences matter a lot to me:
(1) Braun seems to be stronger. The Nood one is barely a pinch on the highest setting. On the highest setting with Braun, I get stronger "rubber band snap" feeling, similar to how it is a professional session. The most effective results - in this case based on stronger light - is always the most important.
(2) The flashes in auto mode on Braun are more than twice as rapid. This means my sessions on Braun can be complete twice as fast as the Nood. These are already time consuming so having such a delay between flashes is definitely a deal breaker for me.

Overall, both are fine, and I am thrilled I discovered IPL so I no longer have prickly porcupine legs and bikini all the time, but I will be returning this one in favor of Braun!

The active ingredient in this TAGAMET ACID REDUCER (6 Tablets; 200 mg Cimetidine per Tablet) is cimetidine, which unfortunately interacts with a lot of prescription medications (especially warfarin, theophylline, phenytoin), and may cause a lot of moderate to serious side effects (nausea, irregular heartbeat, hallucinations, etc.). If you intend to use Tagamet on a regular basis, be sure to google the drug to get complete information about interactions and side effects (try WebMD, Drugs, etc.).

For me, Tagamet is useful when I get acid reflux or a sour stomach that doesn’t respond to antacid chews, and it’s too soon to start another course of Prilosec to deal with chronic excess stomach acid. Tagamet is a “one-shot” pill that helps with the immediate problem.

To relieve symptoms, the dosage is 1 tablet with a glass of water. To prevent symptoms, the dosage is 1 tablet with a glass of water right before consuming foods that cause symptoms. You can take up to 2 tablets in a 24-hour period.

-My gaming friends said it doesn't sound as good as the wired version in discord.

The 10,000 mg/H rating is based on feeding this machine with pure oxygen and with no humidity. Real-world output is probably about 1/10th the rating. Feeding it with normal oxygen levels in air, the rating would be about 1/5th. With the most common humidity levels, it will be half-again. Humidity will greatly dimish the output of this corona discharge type machine. Considering the lower than claimed output, this machine's output is still suitable for shock treatment of small spaces like an automobile interior or single residential rooms.

The timer is inadequate. It features really useless 10 minute increments and only goes up to 120 minutes maximum. Appropriate timing for ozone treatment would be 2, 4, 8, 12, 24 and 48 hours. Ten minute intervals are really useless.

The "Hold" feature would be appropriate for treatments intended for greater than two hours, but this raises a couple of concerns. First, a person has to enter the ozonated space to turn the machine off, but more importantly, the uncertainty of the safety of running this machine unattended for long durations. If the machine were UL Listed, there would be some confidence that it's been rigorously tested for safety and isn't likely to burn the house down while it's running for many hours and no one is home.

The final point I want to make is that this type of corona discharge machine also produces gaseous nitric acid in addition to ozone. While ozone has a fairly short half-life and not much of it is likely to linger for more than a day even in an unventilated space, nitric acid can create a more persistent odor that could last for several weeks.

All told, this ozone generator seems like a good value if it will be used in very low humidity environments and where the space is relatively small (bedroom size or less).

This FOX RUN PASTA DRYING RACK (11654; 18.5", Red) has the cleverest space-saving design that I’ve ever run across in a kitchen gadget! Third, there is a pasta wand (for placing cut pasta on the rods) that stores inside the central support pole. When stored, you don’t even know that it’s there, because it hardly adds any height.

The rack is NOT dishwasher safe, and it’s a bit awkward to clean because the drying arms are round and are attached to the central support pole. However, it wipes clean with a dry cloth or with a dry brush.

Best Buy or any of the other retailers who carry such units and give them all a listen and look at the features they offer and then buy the one that meets your needs in terms of both sound quality and features. Having said that, for me the Roar has more features than any of the
competing units. That is simply fact and not opinion. Most of the products that are in this category seem to be made well but in my opinion, the Roar seems to be made just a little sturdier. I haven't tested that notion by dropping my Roar on the floor but in my hands it simply feels
more robust. Back to the sound question.....since I seriously doubt that many users of portable bluetooth speakers plan on doing serious
listening that entails sitting in a quite room and doing nothing but listening intently to these little portable speakers, consider how they will actually be used. Most people are playing them as background music while they are doing other things such as sitting on the beach or
cooking on the grill or in the kitchen, etc. Critical listening ain't happening here. So let's not talk about sound imaging or speaker spatiality etc. That said, for me, I don't like speakers that have a bass response that overwhelms everything else. I want a more natural sound, One that is

more balanced to my ear. Because of that, I will gravitate towards something like the Roar. If you are one who wants more bass, then you will assuredly better like the sound of any Bose product as they have made a fortune producing bass heavy products for the last 50 years. Again, for me, the features are a big deal and the Roar excels inn that regard. I won't waste your time talking about them as you can look such things up just as easily. And price is a big deal to me. The Roar 1 can be had for $99 now.... so I bought one. The Bose is $299 the last time I checked,...three times the cost of the Roar. So simply put, I loved the price of the Roar, the feature list is unmatched, it feels like military grade construction and lastly, I thought the sound was GOOD. That's why I bought it.

I'm very pleased with this pill organizer. The design is excellent and thoughtful -- the person who designed it clearly had experience using a pill organizer since it gets everything right.

All of the compartments are clearly labeled. The tray for each day lifts out of the holder to make it easier to get the pills out, and snaps back in securely so that it does not come out when you don't want it to. The day of the week is printed on each tray plus on the holder, so there's no risk of messing things up should you take out more than one tray at at time. The text for the day of the week and AM/PM is large and easy to see. All the AM compartments have yellow lids; all the PM ones have blue lids, providing another visual cue as to which is which.

The compartments are roomy enough for every large supplements. The lids snap closed securely but are not difficult to open even with my arthritic hands. The overall build quality is excellent, with everything having a solid, quality feel.

This is as close to a perfect design than I've ever come across so far. Wish I could give it more than 5 stars!
